annotation_description: Leading with Ancient Tomb over Urza's Saga is debatable. Urza's Saga on turn 1 gets the lore counter rolling, provides colorless mana on the same turn, and starts building toward the chapter III tutor or chapter II construct tokens. Ancient Tomb deals 2 damage each time it's tapped. With Blood Moon in hand, there's an argument for Ancient Tomb (tap for 2 colorless, then play Urza's Saga next turn before Blood Moon turns it into a Mountain on turn 2-3). However, the player has Simian Spirit Guide in hand, so a strong line would be: Turn 1 Urza's Saga (gets lore counter I, can tap for {C}), Turn 2 Ancient Tomb + Simian Spirit Guide exile = {C}{C} + {R} = Blood Moon on turn 2, locking the opponent's Flooded Strand. Playing Ancient Tomb first delays Urza's Saga's saga counter progression by a turn. That said, Ancient Tomb first does allow a turn 2 Blood Moon with just Ancient Tomb + SSG (tap Tomb for {C}{C} + exile SSG for {R}), which is the same speed. The key difference is Urza's Saga gets its counters ticking sooner. Since Blood Moon will eventually destroy Urza's Saga by making it a Mountain (losing its saga abilities), the sequencing around Blood Moon matters. Overall this is close but leading Urza's Saga may have been slightly better to start the saga clock.

With Ancient Tomb already on the battlefield providing 2 colorless mana, plus Simian Spirit Guide exiled from hand for 1 red mana, the player has exactly 3 mana (2 colorless + 1 red) to cast Blood Moon on turn 1. Blood Moon turns all nonbasic lands into Mountains, which would devastate the opponent's mana base (their Flooded Strand and any future fetchlands/duals become Mountains). Instead, the player chose to cast Simian Spirit Guide as a 2/2 creature for 3 mana, which is a terrible rate and wastes the Spirit Guide's primary utility as a free mana source. A turn 1 Blood Moon is one of the most powerful plays in Legacy and could essentially lock the opponent out of the game.

With Ancient Tomb (producing 2 colorless) plus Simian Spirit Guide (exiling from hand for 1 red), the player has access to 3 mana including 1 red - exactly enough to cast Blood Moon (2R). Blood Moon on turn 1 would turn the opponent's Flooded Strand (and any future nonbasic lands) into Mountains, potentially locking a blue-based opponent out of the game entirely. This is one of the most powerful plays available in Legacy with a prison deck. The player's reasoning incorrectly states they can't play anything, but Blood Moon costs {2}{R} and is castable with Ancient Tomb + Simian Spirit Guide exile.

With Ancient Tomb producing {C}{C} and Simian Spirit Guide exiling for {R}, the player had access to 3 mana (2 colorless + 1 red), which is exactly enough to cast Blood Moon (2R). Blood Moon would turn the opponent's Flooded Strand (and any future nonbasic lands) into Mountains, potentially locking them out of blue mana. This is a devastating Turn 1 play against a blue deck running fetchlands. The player incorrectly assessed they couldn't cast anything beyond what Ancient Tomb alone provides.

With Ancient Tomb already on the battlefield providing {C}{C}, and Simian Spirit Guide available for exile to add {R}, the player has access to 3 mana (2 colorless + 1 red) which is exactly enough to cast Blood Moon ({2}{R}). The opponent has only a Flooded Strand (a nonbasic land) on board and is likely playing a blue deck with fetchlands and dual lands. Resolving Blood Moon on turn 2 would turn all nonbasic lands into Mountains, devastating the opponent's mana base and potentially locking them out of the game. Playing Urza's Saga instead is far less impactful — it just adds a colorless mana this turn and doesn't pressure the opponent's resources. Furthermore, Blood Moon will eventually turn Urza's Saga into a Mountain (losing its saga abilities) if cast later, so playing Saga before Blood Moon is anti-synergistic unless you plan to never cast Blood Moon.

The player exiled Simian Spirit Guide from hand to add {R}, but there's no indication they used that mana for anything meaningful this turn. Simian Spirit Guide is a 2/2 creature that costs {2}{R} to cast normally, and the player's reasoning mentions wanting to 'get that Spirit Guide down' as a creature, but exiling it only produces mana - it doesn't put it on the battlefield. The player seems to have confused exiling SSG (which just adds {R} to mana pool) with casting it as a creature. This wastes a card for no benefit, as the {R} produced will go unused if nothing else is cast this turn. With Ancient Tomb providing {C}{C}, they could have cast Blood Moon (costs {2}{R}) by using Ancient Tomb + exiling SSG, which would be a powerful play turning the opponent's Flooded Strand into a Mountain. But simply exiling SSG with no follow-up spell is pure card disadvantage.

With Ancient Tomb (producing 2 colorless) and Urza's Saga chapter I (producing 1 colorless), the player has 3 colorless mana available. Blood Moon costs {2}{R} so it cannot be cast without red mana, but the player could potentially evoke a Fury by exiling the other Fury (a red card) from hand. More importantly, the reasoning is completely delusional - mentioning 'Ragavan and Spirit Guide' on board when neither exists, and claiming Blood Moon is 'ready' when there's no red mana source to cast it. The player passed without casting anything, but with 3 mana available and The One Ring costing 4, they genuinely cannot cast anything useful this turn since Ancient Tomb and Urza's Saga only produce colorless. However, they could evoke Fury (exile the other red card - Fury, Blood Moon, or Pyrogoyf from hand) targeting the opponent's face... wait, Fury only hits creatures/planeswalkers. So passing is actually reasonable given the mana constraints. The reasoning is hallucinated nonsense but the actual decision to pass is defensible since no castable spells exist with only colorless mana.

Against an Ancient Tomb + Urza's Saga deck (classic Stompy/Prison shell), Blood Moon is a very real threat. The opponent can cast Blood Moon as early as next turn with Ancient Tomb + any land. If Blood Moon resolves, Underground Sea and Flooded Strand both become Mountains, leaving the player with zero access to U or B mana and stranding their entire hand.

Casting Brainstorm during own main phase taps Underground Sea, which means Daze cannot be cast this turn (no untapped Island to return). The opponent has Ancient Tomb + Urza's Saga for 4 mana and could cast The One Ring or Blood Moon. Additionally, playing a fetch land (Scalding Tarn) first before Brainstorm would provide a second shuffle source.

message: Select a card from a graveyard
annotation_description: When choosing which card to exile with Soul-Guide Lantern's ETB trigger, the player exiled Brainstorm instead of Bloodstained Mire. Against a storm/combo deck running Lion's Eye Diamond, the key consideration is threshold for Cabal Ritual (which needs 7 cards in graveyard). Both cards reduce the graveyard count equally (from 2 to 1), so the threshold consideration is neutral. However, Bloodstained Mire is a fetchland that could be relevant if the opponent has cards that interact with lands in graveyards (like Crucible of Worlds), while Brainstorm is already cast and unlikely to matter from the graveyard. In Legacy storm/combo matchups, neither choice matters much since the graveyard cards aren't being reused, but exiling the fetchland is marginally better against potential graveyard recursion strategies.

With Lion's Eye Diamond on the battlefield and Cabal Rituals in hand, the player appears to be on a storm/combo deck. Casting Consider here is reasonable for card selection, but Brainstorm is arguably better in this spot since it draws 3 cards and lets you put back 2, giving much deeper card selection. With fetchlands available (Flooded Strand and Scalding Tarn), Brainstorm can be shuffled away for maximum value. Consider only sees 1 card deeper. The opponent has Urza's Saga which will create a construct token soon, so finding combo pieces quickly is important. Brainstorm + fetch gives 3 fresh cards versus Consider's 1, and both cost U.

Casting Brainstorm in response to their own Consider is suboptimal sequencing. By resolving Consider first, then casting Brainstorm afterward, they could use the fetch lands (Flooded Strand/Scalding Tarn) to shuffle away the two cards put back on top with Brainstorm. Casting Brainstorm before Consider resolves means Consider's surveil only bins one of the put-back cards, leaving the other stuck on top without a shuffle.

Playing Cavern of Souls when there are no creatures in hand and it only produces colorless mana. Flooded Strand would provide more flexible mana (can fetch blue or black sources), can be bounced for Daze, and better supports the spells in hand (Brainstorm, Force of Will, Cabal Ritual, Daze).

Cracking Flooded Strand before Brainstorm resolves is suboptimal sequencing. The classic Brainstorm-fetchland interaction requires letting Brainstorm resolve first (draw 3, put 2 bad cards back), then cracking the fetchland to shuffle away the unwanted cards. While they have Scalding Tarn as a backup fetchland for post-Brainstorm shuffling, this line wastes a fetchland that could be preserved for future use.

Cracking Scalding Tarn before Brainstorm resolves wastes the classic Brainstorm+fetchland shuffle interaction. They have Flooded Strand in hand that could serve as the post-Brainstorm shuffle if they waited, but by using Scalding Tarn now they're fetching a land unnecessarily before seeing their Brainstorm draws. The correct line is to let Brainstorm resolve, put back 2 unwanted cards, then play Flooded Strand and crack it to shuffle away those cards.

Casting Cabal Ritual with Brainstorm on the stack is suspicious. The classic line with LED + Brainstorm is to crack LED in response to Brainstorm (retaining the draws), but casting Cabal Ritual instead may waste the opportunity for optimal sequencing. With Underground Sea tapped, paying for Cabal Ritual likely requires cracking LED (discarding Force of Will and Daze as protection), and the mana generation may not lead to a meaningful play this turn.

message: Select a Plains or Island card
annotation_description: Against a red prison deck that likely runs Blood Moon (Ancient Tomb, Chrome Mox, Simian Spirit Guide archetype), fetching Underground Sea instead of basic Island leaves the player with zero basic lands. Under Blood Moon, all their nonbasic lands become Mountains, cutting them off from both blue and black mana entirely. They already have one Underground Sea in play for black mana access.

Casting Cabal Ritual before Brainstorm is poor sequencing. Brainstorm should be cast first to see three new cards and potentially find better uses for the mana or a combo piece. Cabal Ritual produces BBB (no threshold yet with only 4 cards in graveyard), but there's nothing obvious to spend it on in hand besides Daze and Force of Will (which are free counters). The BBB mana will likely go to waste. Additionally, casting Brainstorm first would let the player put back unwanted cards (like the Cabal Ritual itself if it's not needed) and find something more impactful. There's also a Flooded Strand and Polluted Delta in hand that could shuffle away cards put back with Brainstorm.

Opponent cast Cabal Ritual, which generates BBB (or BBBBB with threshold). With 5 cards in opponent's graveyard (after this resolves it would be close to threshold), this mana could fuel a devastating play like a turn-5 combo piece or The One Ring. Kimi25 Analyst had both Daze and Force of Will available to counter the Cabal Ritual but instead chose to cast Brainstorm, which doesn't counter the spell. The Cabal Ritual resolved, giving the opponent a burst of black mana. Brainstorm doesn't interact with the stack in any meaningful way here - it just draws cards while letting a dangerous mana ritual resolve.

Fury is being hardcast for 3RR (5 mana) when the player only has Ancient Tomb and Chrome Mox on the battlefield, which can produce at most 3 mana (2 colorless from Ancient Tomb + 1 red from Chrome Mox with Simian Spirit Guide imprinted). The player likely needs to exile Simian Spirit Guide from hand for the additional red mana, spending 4 total mana sources for a 3/3 double striker. More importantly, Blood Moon would be devastating here - the opponent has Underground Sea x2 and Cavern of Souls as their lands, all nonbasic. Blood Moon turns them all into Mountains, cutting them off from black and blue mana entirely, likely locking them out of the game. Blood Moon costs 2R which is exactly castable with Ancient Tomb (2 colorless) + exile Simian Spirit Guide (R), or Ancient Tomb + Chrome Mox. Casting Fury instead of Blood Moon misses a potentially game-winning lock piece in favor of a beater.

Fury's ETB has no creature/planeswalker targets on the opponent's board, so the only value is the 3/3 double strike body. Evoking Fury (even though ETB has no good targets) and preserving resources for Blood Moon could be more impactful.

annotation_description: Evoking Fury when the opponent has zero creatures or planeswalkers on the battlefield. Fury's ETB can only deal damage to creatures and/or planeswalkers, so with no valid targets the ability does nothing. The evoked Fury is then immediately sacrificed. This wastes two cards (Fury + the exiled red card) for absolutely no effect.

When discarding to hand size, the player chose Pyrogoyf over Simian Spirit Guide. With Ancient Tomb and Chrome Mox as the only mana sources, the player needs additional mana to cast their spells. However, Simian Spirit Guide provides a one-time red mana from exile, which could help cast Blood Moon (2R) next turn alongside Ancient Tomb. Meanwhile, Pyrogoyf is a 4-mana creature that's harder to cast and could be relevant as a finisher. The duplicate Pyrogoyf is arguably less useful than Simian Spirit Guide given the current mana situation - the player already has one Pyrogoyf and two Furies as threats. That said, Simian Spirit Guide's exile-for-mana ability means it doesn't need to be in hand at the start of the turn - it can be used any time. The player may want to keep it for flexibility. This is close to a wash since both cards have arguments for being discarded, but keeping the mana source seems slightly better given the constrained mana base.

Playing Flooded Strand before casting Brainstorm is a sequencing error. Brainstorm allows you to draw 3 cards and put 2 back on top of your library. If you cast Brainstorm first (using Underground Sea), you could then use Flooded Strand to shuffle away the two unwanted cards you put back on top, getting a 'free' shuffle effect that dramatically improves Brainstorm's value. By playing Flooded Strand first (presumably to fetch and then Brainstorm), you lose the ability to use it as a shuffle effect after Brainstorm. The player already has Polluted Delta in hand which could serve as a post-Brainstorm shuffle, but playing the Flooded Strand as the land drop consumes it before Brainstorm resolves, and the player still has an untapped Underground Sea to cast Brainstorm from.

Fetched with Flooded Strand before casting Brainstorm, wasting the classic Brainstorm+fetch synergy. By fetching first, the player cannot shuffle away the 2 cards put back on top of the library with Brainstorm, significantly reducing Brainstorm's card selection power.

Opponent is at 8 life post-Doomsday and will likely win next turn with their constructed pile. Blood Moon is castable (Ancient Tomb for 2 colorless + Chrome Mox for red) and would turn both Underground Seas into Mountains, cutting off the opponent's black mana from lands. This could be devastating for a Doomsday pile that likely needs black mana to execute. Playing Urza's Saga provides no immediate disruption against an imminent combo kill.

Exiled Simian Spirit Guide from hand for {R} mana that apparently wasn't used for anything, wasting a card. The opponent just resolved Doomsday and is at 8 life with a 5-card library - this is a critical turn to disrupt or pressure them.

Against a post-Doomsday opponent at 8 life with Underground Seas and Cavern of Souls providing their mana, Blood Moon could shut off their access to black mana (leaving only Island + Mountains + LED), potentially stranding their carefully constructed Doomsday pile. The opponent needs to execute their pile precisely and disrupting their mana could be game-winning.

Pyrogoyf on the stack will ETB dealing 5 damage (5 card types in graveyards: artifact, enchantment, land, creature, sorcery). At 8 life post-Doomsday, taking 5 to the face drops to 3 life with a 5/6 creature threatening lethal next combat. All opponent's lands are tapped, making Daze essentially a hard counter here.

KimiK2 Gramps had a Pyrogoyf ETB trigger (from casting/entering a second Pyrogoyf or from Fury's evoke) that deals damage equal to its power to any target. The opponent is at 8 life and Pyrogoyf's power is 5 (based on card types in graveyards). Instead of directing 5 damage at the opponent (putting them to 3 life, within lethal range), they targeted their own Pyrogoyf, effectively wasting the damage and killing their own creature. With the opponent at 8 life, directing damage to face is clearly superior, especially since Pyrogoyf was their primary attacker.

Kimi25 Analyst is at 2 life facing a Pyrogoyf and other threats, with Dark Ritual on the stack. Dark Ritual will give the opponent BBB mana, which could enable casting Blood Moon or other devastating spells. The opponent already has a Pyrogoyf that can attack for lethal next turn (with 3+ card types in graveyards giving it at least 3 power). Allowing Dark Ritual to resolve gives the opponent massive mana advantage to deploy more threats or disruption. With Daze and two Force of Wills in hand, countering Dark Ritual (via Daze returning an Island, or Force of Will exiling a blue card) would deny the opponent mana and potentially buy a critical turn. At 2 life, every turn matters and denying the opponent's mana development is crucial. The player appears to have cast Doomsday (it's in their graveyard) meaning they're on a Doomsday pile plan, but they have no draw spell in hand - they need to survive to draw into their pile. Letting Dark Ritual resolve when the opponent could use that mana to deploy a lethal threat or Blood Moon is game-losing.

At 2 life, casting Force of Will (which costs 1 life via alternate cost) on Dark Ritual would put Analyst to 1 life, and wastes a hard counter on mana acceleration rather than the actual threat. More critically, with 2 Force of Wills in hand, Analyst can counter whatever payoff spell Gramps casts with the Dark Ritual mana. Dark Ritual itself doesn't threaten lethal.
